headings.title: Introduction to Health Economics and Scarcity
headings.content: Health economics applies economic principles to the allocation of resources in the health sector. Resources such as skilled nursing personnel, hospital beds, advanced diagnostic machinery, and pharmaceutical supplies are inherently limited. Meanwhile, human health needs and desires are virtually limitless. This mismatch creates the fundamental problem of **scarcity**. Because society cannot produce every healthcare service desired, choices must be made regarding resource distribution. Economic evaluation helps healthcare systems determine which interventions offer the greatest value and health gain for the finite funds available.

headings.title: Opportunity Cost
headings.content: Every choice made in clinical practice and healthcare management carries an **opportunity cost**, defined as the value of the next best alternative foregone when a resource is utilized. If a district health board allocates its budget to build a new specialist surgical theatre, those exact funds cannot be used to expand community primary healthcare clinics or purchase essential obstetric supplies. In everyday nursing administration, spending limited hours on non-clinical paperwork means sacrificing direct patient bedside care. Recognizing opportunity cost forces decision-makers to evaluate whether a chosen intervention is truly worth more than the alternatives sacrificed.

headings.title: Demand for Health Care
headings.content:
Demand in health economics refers to the quantity of healthcare services that individuals are willing and able to purchase at various price points. Unlike traditional consumer goods, healthcare demand is often irregular, unpredictable, and driven by clinical need rather than pure consumer preference. Several factors shape this demand curve:

- **Price and Insurance**: Higher out-of-pocket costs typically reduce the quantity demanded, while comprehensive health insurance coverage lowers the perceived price at the point of service, often increasing utilization.
- **Health Status**: Individuals with chronic conditions or poorer baseline health naturally demand a higher volume of medical interventions.
- **Income Levels**: Higher disposable income generally increases the ability to pay for elective and preventive health services.
- **Perceived Need and Education**: Health literacy and understanding of disease risks directly influence whether an individual seeks professional care.

headings.title: Supply of Health Care
headings.content:
Supply represents the total quantity of healthcare services, goods, and professional hours that providers are willing and able to offer at different price levels. In the health sector, supply is heavily regulated and constrained by long training pipelines for doctors and nurses, strict licensing requirements, and high capital costs for infrastructure.

- **Provider Availability**: The density and distribution of trained healthcare professionals directly dictate service capacity.
- **Technological Advances**: New medical devices and pharmaceuticals expand the scope of what can be supplied, though often at higher costs.
- **Input Costs**: The price of medical consumables, facility maintenance, and competitive wages for staff shift the overall supply curve.

headings.title: Economic Price and Out-of-Pocket Costs
headings.content: The economic price of healthcare encompasses more than just the numbered figure on a clinic bill. It includes direct medical expenses such as medications, laboratory tests, and consultation fees, alongside indirect costs like transportation to a facility and lost wages during recovery. In many developing regions, high out-of-pocket pricing creates catastrophic health expenditures, pushing vulnerable households into poverty when illness strikes. Understanding these financial barriers helps nurses anticipate why patients might default on treatment regimens or delay seeking necessary professional care.

headings.title: Market Equilibrium
headings.content: Market equilibrium occurs when the quantity of healthcare services demanded by consumers precisely equals the quantity supplied by providers. At this intersection point, the market clears without persistent shortages or surpluses. However, true free-market equilibrium is rarely achieved in healthcare due to market failures such as asymmetric information, where providers know far more about clinical needs than patients do, and heavy government intervention. When prices are artificially distorted by subsidies or price controls, surpluses or severe deficits in service availability frequently emerge.

headings.title: Externalities in Health Care
headings.content: An externality arises when the consumption or production of a good affects third parties who are not directly involved in the transaction. Health interventions frequently generate positive externalities that benefit society as a whole. For example, childhood immunization not only protects the vaccinated child but also creates herd immunity, shielding vulnerable community members who cannot receive vaccines. Because individuals may under-invest in preventive services if they only consider their personal benefit, governments often subsidize or mandate these public health interventions to achieve optimal societal well-being.
